name: Right arm electrode
landmark: Right infraclavicular fossa, or the right forearm/wrist
howToFind: Feel the lateral third of the right clavicle and place the electrode just below it over the deltopectoral groove, on flat skin away from bone and large muscle bellies.
why: RA is the negative pole of leads I and II and the positive pole of aVR. Because the limb leads record the frontal plane, moving this electrode rotates the entire calculated axis — the commonest reason a computer reports an 'axis deviation' that is not real.
views: Frontal plane — contributes to leads I, II, III, aVR and aVL
pitfalls: Swapping RA and LA inverts lead I and produces a global negative in lead I with an upright aVR — a classic artefact mistaken for dextrocardia
Placing it over the deltoid muscle belly adds movement artefact
Torso placement shortens the recorded limb-lead amplitudes; keep placement consistent between serial ECGs

name: Left arm electrode
landmark: Left infraclavicular fossa, or the left forearm/wrist
howToFind: Mirror the right arm electrode: just below the lateral third of the left clavicle, on flat skin.
why: LA is the positive pole of lead I and the negative pole of lead III. With RA and LL it forms Einthoven's triangle, whose geometry is the basis of the entire frontal-plane axis calculation.
views: Frontal plane — contributes to leads I, II, III, aVR and aVL
pitfalls: Reversal with RA is the single commonest limb-lead error
Asymmetric placement between the two arms distorts the axis
Avoid placing over an arteriovenous fistula or a lymphoedematous limb

name: Right leg electrode (neutral)
landmark: Right lower abdomen or right leg, below the level of the umbilicus
howToFind: Place on the right lower abdominal wall or the right thigh — anywhere below the umbilicus and away from bony prominences.
why: RL does not contribute to any recorded lead. It is the driven right-leg electrode: the amplifier feeds an inverted version of the common-mode signal back through it, actively cancelling mains interference. Removing it does not change the waveform's shape but does make the trace noisy.
pitfalls: Often blamed for artefact when in fact it is the electrode preventing it
Poor skin contact here degrades every lead at once
Reversal with LL produces a near-flat lead II

name: Left leg electrode
landmark: Left lower abdomen or left leg, below the level of the umbilicus
howToFind: Mirror the right leg electrode on the left lower abdominal wall or left thigh.
why: LL is the positive pole of leads II, III and aVF — the three inferior leads. Together they look at the inferior wall of the left ventricle, so this electrode is what makes an inferior infarct visible.
views: Inferior wall — leads II, III and aVF
pitfalls: Reversal with RL flattens lead II
Placing it too high on the abdomen adds respiratory baseline wander
Consistency matters for serial comparison in a patient with evolving inferior changes

name: Precordial lead V1
landmark: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
howToFind: Find the suprasternal notch, slide down to the ridge of the sternal angle — that is the second costal cartilage and the second rib. Walk down: second space, third rib, third space, fourth rib, fourth space. Place V1 immediately to the right of the sternum in that fourth space.
why: V1 sits directly over the right ventricle and interventricular septum, so it is the lead that reports septal activation, right-sided conduction and right ventricular strain. It is where the bundle branch block pattern, the P wave morphology and posterior infarction as tall R waves are read.
views: Septum and right ventricle — with V2, the anteroseptal wall
pitfalls: Placed too high — a common error — V1 and V2 record an rSr′ pattern and inverted T waves that mimic septal infarction or Brugada pattern
Counting from the clavicle instead of the sternal angle causes systematic misplacement
V1 and V2 misplacement is the most frequently repeated electrode error in practice

name: Precordial lead V2
landmark: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
howToFind: Directly opposite V1, on the left side of the sternum in the same fourth intercostal space. The two should sit level with each other.
why: V2 overlies the anteroseptal wall and gives the largest S wave of the precordial leads in most people. It is central to R wave progression across the chest, and with V1 it is where posterior infarction is detected as tall R waves and ST depression.
pitfalls: High placement produces poor R wave progression and pseudo-infarct patterns
V1 and V2 placed above the fourth space can imitate anteroseptal infarction or a Brugada pattern
Check that V1 and V2 are level with each other, not stepped

name: Precordial lead V3
landmark: Midway between V2 and V4, on a straight line between them
howToFind: Place V4 first, then position V3 at the midpoint of the line joining V2 and V4. It is the only electrode defined by other electrodes rather than by an anatomical landmark.
why: V3 covers the anterior wall and the transition zone, where the QRS changes from predominantly negative to predominantly positive across the precordium. Its position is derived, so an error in V4 automatically displaces V3 as well.
views: Anterior wall — the precordial transition zone
pitfalls: Placing V3 before V4 guarantees it ends up in the wrong place
It is the usual site for prominent U waves in hypokalaemia, so misplacement can hide them
Small displacements alter R wave progression and can suggest anterior infarction

name: Precordial lead V4
landmark: Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
howToFind: Find the midpoint of the left clavicle and drop a vertical line from it. Follow the fourth space found for V1 and V2 down over the next rib into the fifth space, and place V4 where that space crosses the midclavicular line. In women, place it on the chest wall beneath the breast, not on breast tissue.
why: V4 sits over the cardiac apex and the anterior and apical left ventricular wall, so it is the reference point for the whole lateral group — V5 and V6 are placed on its horizontal level, not by following the curve of the ribs. Getting V4 wrong therefore displaces three leads at once.
pitfalls: Placing V4 in the fourth space is the commonest single precordial error and shifts V5 and V6 with it
Placing electrodes on breast tissue attenuates the signal and reduces reproducibility — go under the breast
Following the rib line rather than a horizontal plane sends V5 and V6 too low

name: Precordial lead V5
landmark: Left anterior axillary line, horizontally level with V4
howToFind: Draw an imaginary horizontal line from V4 around the chest. Place V5 where that line meets the anterior axillary fold — not by counting ribs again.
why: V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall of the left ventricle, supplied largely by the circumflex artery. V5 also carries the largest R wave in most people, so it is used in voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy.
views: Lateral wall of the left ventricle
pitfalls: Placing V5 by rib-counting instead of on V4's horizontal level puts it too low
Inconsistent placement between recordings invalidates serial comparison of lateral ST changes
Voltage criteria for hypertrophy are meaningless if V5 is misplaced

name: Precordial lead V6
landmark: Left mid-axillary line, horizontally level with V4 and V5
howToFind: Continue the same horizontal line laterally to the mid-axillary line — the vertical line dropped from the apex of the axilla. With the arm at the side, this is roughly in line with the middle of the armpit.
why: V6 is the most lateral of the standard chest leads and, with V5 and lead I, forms the lateral group. It usually shows a tall R with a small Q from normal septal depolarisation, and the loss of that septal Q is itself a clue to conduction disease.
views: Lateral wall of the left ventricle
pitfalls: Placed too posteriorly it produces artificially small complexes
Placed too low it exaggerates the apparent inferior extension of lateral changes
Should be level with V4 and V5, forming a horizontal row, not a curve
